title: Teacher who sexually abused pupil back in Indonesia jail after BBC investigation
content: A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early. Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher. A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know. On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief. "I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC. The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations. But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review. That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison. Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions". "We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said. For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication. "I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said. Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15. "I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said. She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her. She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened". Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube . Watching BBC undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, when he should still have been in prison, Ira became tearful. "It's like nothing ever happened," she said. Ira was invited to a parliamentary hearing this week into the state's handling of sexual abuse cases in religious and educational institutions, held in response to the BBC's investigation. Lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has represented several victims of abuse in educational institutions, also addressed the hearing and said authorities were often reluctant to investigate allegations of abuse because they involved "influential religious figures who have large followings". He told the hearing that he regularly faced threats and intimidation as a result of taking on such cases. Bechi is the son of prominent Islamic cleric Muhammad Mukhtar Mu'thi, founder of the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in Jombang, East Java. He was arrested in 2022 after a 15-hour police siege at the school, where supporters had gathered to prevent his arrest. Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence after Bechi was accused of rape by a number of students, but he was acquitted of the rape charges and convicted of the lesser sexual assault offence of one student. The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah boarding school as part of its investigation but received no response. title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
content: When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India. India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan. That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later. Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport. Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats. Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless. Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience. The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana. In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer. Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago. Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world. Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped. Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains. Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on. Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post. "I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote. "Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again. "Captaincy ends, the journey continues." Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future. In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision. The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket. Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones. Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age. Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai. The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development. She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since. An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills. Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome. That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name. The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history. Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup. Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals. India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket. With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate. title: Royal Navy sailor in court accused of preparing to spy for Russia
content: A junior Royal Navy sailor accused of preparing to spy for Russia has appeared in court. Able Seaman Teddy Young, who specialised in warfare intelligence, allegedly retained UK defence and intelligence material that he had access to and made preparations to disclose sensitive information, a court was told. The 24-year-old appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday after being charged under the National Security Act. The BBC understands that the allegations against Young include translating a message into Russian and looking for a web portal that invited people to submit information to Russia. Wearing a police-issue grey sweatshirt, Young spoke in court to confirm his name, date of birth and his address in Clapham, near Bedford. He is formally charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for disclosing protected information, and obtaining, copying, recording or retaining protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power. The charges cover a period between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025. "The allegation is that while serving as a Royal Navy warfare intelligence rating with high level security clearance and intelligence-system access, Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young accessed and retained sensitive UK defence and intelligence material and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power," the Crown Prosecution Service told the court in a written summary of the allegations. Police said the alleged offences were not related to the recent RAF Fairford incident that resulted in a number of arrests after suspicious activity was reported near the base. In total, seven men have been arrested and later released on bail in connection with the incident, which is being investigated by counter-terror police. Young was arrested at his home address in Bedfordshire on Tuesday. He is the first member of the armed forces to be charged under the new National Security Act 2023. Cdr Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. "We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter." A Royal Navy spokesperson confirmed a service member had been charged and added: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage." Judge Annabel Pilling remanded Young in custody. He will next appear at the Old Bailey on 16 October. The grave of the "proud Yorkshireman" is updated with his name at a ceremony in the Netherlands. title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign sign
content: Warning: This article contains details which some readers may find distressing. A congressional candidate in Arizona has said she was raped in a car park as she repaired campaign signs late at night in her district. Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a Democrat, told the Phoenix New Times she was knocked unconscious during the alleged attack in the Phoenix suburb of Sun City on 14 August, waking up to find a man on top of her. She said she did not initially notify police until filing a report with the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office two weeks later. Her Republican opponent, Abraham Hamadeh, urged authorities in a statement to "investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place". "No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community," said Hamadeh, who is running for a second term in office. Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times she was "embarrassed" and "just wanted to forget", but felt compelled stand up for other victims. The candidate said she often speaks on the campaign trail about fighting for Arizonans. She told the Phoenix New Times: "I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault." The BBC has contacted the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office for comment. A sheriff's spokesman told the New York Times the investigation was ongoing. After the attack, Greene-Placentia said she withdrew from the public for two days, staying in an apartment separate from her husband and skipping a campaign event. When she emerged, her husband, campaign staff and others in her circle noticed she was acting differently, according to Phoenix New Times. Greene-Placentia said she did not see a doctor following the alleged attack in congressional district eight and did not receive a sexual assault examination. She said her memory of what happened was spotty and she did not get a good look at either of the two assailants, but described them as white men, according to the New York Times. She told the Phoenix New Times that one assailant may have made a comment about her political affiliation, together with a misogynistic slur, although she could not be certain. The candidate said she was concerned voters might think it was a political stunt to win points in a heavily Republican district. She also expressed concern that the allegations might overshadow her messaging around affordability. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide . A list of UK organisations that can help is available here . title: US deportations to African countries unlawful and exploit suffering - rights group
content: Campaign group Human Rights Watch (HRW) says the deportation of migrants from the US to third-party African countries is against the law and exploits suffering to deter migration. "Many, if not most" of the deportees have no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there, HRW says in a report. Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, more than 500 people have been sent to African countries where they are not citizens, the group says, citing US data. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said "third country removals are an essential public safety tool that remove the most dangerous criminal illegal aliens from our streets". Tackling immigration was one of Trump's key pledges during the 2024 election. Eswatini, which welcomed 32 deportees from the US, says three people - from Yemen, Belize and Laos - "voluntarily departed" to their home countries recently. According to HRW, some of the countries accepting the deportees have "arbitrarily detained" or sent them to their home countries, where they face "the risk of persecution or torture". The group said that people sent to Eswatini, Ghana and South Sudan, had been arbitrarily detained and faced ill-treatment while in detention. In Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and Ghana, the deportees had been sent to their countries of origin despite the risk of "violating the principle of nonrefoulement [that people should not be sent to a country where they face torture, cruel treatment, or threats to their life and freedom]", it said. The group cited an unnamed US official as having told a Senate hearing that the point for the administration was that it could "threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere". "The point is to scare people," HRW said. "Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration," said Michael Garcia Bochenek, the group's interim US programme director. In a statement from to the BBC, DHS said: "ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] is given diplomatic assurances from destination countries that the illegal aliens being removed there will be safe. When an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them." White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told the BBC that those being sent to third countries were those whose home nations refused to take them or who had court orders preventing them being sent home. "Any illegal alien who wants to go home, we will arrange a free flight for them and give them a $3,000 check," she said. None of the African countries named has commented on the report. However, while announcing the recent departure of three migrants on Wednesday, Eswatini said that it was committed to ensuring that the "rights, dignity and well-being of third-country nationals were respected and protected". HRW said it interviewed 24 third-country nationals in six countries - Cameroon, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan. Some described to the group "abusive treatment" during their deportation flights, including being chained for about 18 hours and with no knowledge of their destination. They were also "denied access to essential medication, and often did not receive sufficient food or water". "The opaque deals that facilitate these transfers, some of which are still secret, are part of a US policy that violates international human rights law," HRW says. According to the report, at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender (LGBT) were sent to African states that criminalise same-sex relations. Among them were refugees granted protection in the US based on the likelihood they would be persecuted back home because of their orientation or gender identity. In November, a Nigerian man deported from the US initially to Ghana expressed his fears to the BBC after he and five others were secretly transferred to Togo. He spoke of his fears about returning to Nigeria, where his association with a separatist activist group could lead to his arrest and torture. In DR Congo, HRW says it was told by a US lawyer that of the 15 people from Colombia, Peru and Ecuador deported to the country in April, none remained there by late September, with 11 having returned to their home countries. "The uncertainty and other conditions they faced in the Democratic Republic of Congo call into question whether these returns to countries of origin were voluntary," the group said. Equatorial Guinea, which received 65 people, quickly sent at least two people to their home countries, HRW said. Burundi announced late last month that it had agreed to take in migrants deported from the US. Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent. title: Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method?
content: The botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory. A week after receiving two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital, she is said to be walking and talking again in limited ways. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation and suspended all executions for the rest of the year. The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area. At a hearing on Wednesday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court. But Pike's lawyers are seeking to have her death sentence commuted to life in prison without parole. Lee, who has commutation powers, has not indicated what the state will do. Slemmer was murdered by both Pike and Pike's then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was not an adult at the time so was spared the death penalty and remains in prison. The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next. The Tennessee Department of Correction could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment. "For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said. Johnson said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of the state’s lethal injection protocol. Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Johnson called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition. Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure. Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Johnson said. Johnson, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method. This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature. Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair." Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging". Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws. She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said. Given that Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there was a scenario in which the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method. It was also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained. Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage. There is a precedent of states finding a different method to execute a death-row inmate. In 2024, Alabama executed a convicted murderer using a different method to the one that was originally planned. Kenneth Eugene Smith was put to death using nitrogen gas - having failed with its initial plan of lethal injection. Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment. Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection - meaning that he has a year-long reprieve. It will therefore probably take a while for any movement in Pike's case. "At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Johnson said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied. Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered. "If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said. There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state. The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed. The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes. Lawyers for Jamaal Howard had asked a judge to pause the execution after Christa Pike's botched lethal injections. The US death row inmate's legal team said at a press conference that she is now "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution. A medical expert advising her legal team says the murderer of Colleen Slemmer is communicating in a "basic way". Nidal Malik Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers and injured another 32 in the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
content: Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools. The movement has turned violent in places – hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people – including an unknown number of outside troublemakers – have been arrested. The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds. "Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves. There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 19:00, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycéen told France 2. France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point. The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalauréat, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque. Those grievances are real. But do they by themselves explain the form the protest movement has taken? How does France compare with other countries? According to a recent report by the OECD, a club of developed nations, the French government spends more per lycée student than the EU average for upper-secondary schools. Teacher shortages are indeed acute, but no worse than elsewhere. By OECD measures they are actually milder – fewer posts go unfilled – although French teachers receive relatively low pay. Schooldays that stretch into the late afternoon are indeed a problem for French pupils. This is the result mostly of long lunch breaks and complex schedules rather than making up for holidays, which are not especially long compared with other EU countries. The extended day has always been a sad fact of French school life and can hardly account for the present eruption. Neither can pressure created by a dysfunctional higher-education system. In most European countries, 80-90% of young people complete secondary education, and competition for good university places creates stress elsewhere too. And while underfunding, dilapidated buildings and fears about the future are behind the students' discontent, those complaints do not by themselves explain why the movement has become "unprecedented" in terms of the number of schools, pupils and the degree of violence involved, in the words of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. The scale of protests is all the more remarkable as those involved are taking considerable risks. Blockading a school or university by threats or force is illegal, and draws in police, as well as casseurs (vandals), and pupils have become caught up in police crowd-control operations that are often heavy handed. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, in his latest message, has insisted security forces are not under orders to "confront high-school students", only to enforce the law. To understand the pupils' tactics, one must look beyond the barricaded school gates to a political tradition. In France, the power has often resided on the street as much as in elected bodies. Students know this as well as anyone else. In October 1990, a rape at a school in Seine-Saint-Denis – an area north of Paris that has been a focus for the present unrest – was the trigger for mass rallies against underfunding and staff shortages. It resulted in the government releasing the equivalent of €1.2bn (£1bn) in today's money for lycées. In October 1998, 500,000 pupils marched across France over similar demands, resulting in almost €1bn to renovate schools and 14,000 extra staff. On several occasions student protests defeated government reforms – such as a university overhaul in 1986 and a lower youth minimum wage in 1994. Probably the most striking display of student power came in 2006, with the withdrawal of a law designed to loosen hire-and-fire rules for those under 26 to try to tackle youth unemployment. The measure, passed by parliament and signed by then-President Jacques Chirac, was scrapped after weeks of blockades in universities and lycées often marred by violence. French adults have shown how blockading roads can prevail over elected officials. The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) uprising of 2018-2019 – which saw shops ransacked and government buildings attacked across the country – led the government to drop a rise in fuel taxes and approve €10bn in spending. The street does not always win. In 1968 – a heroic precedent cited by every French protest movement – a student uprising was actually brought to an end by election. But the lycéens are heirs to a political culture in which demonstrators compete with elected officials to be seen as the legitimate voice of the people. On the face of it, the current balance of power favour the pupils. A poll for BFMTV suggests that that 72% of French people regard their demands as legitimate and 55% support the movement. Backed by many teachers, labour unions and left-wing politicians, the protesters are on the front foot. Another rally is planned for Thursday afternoon. The government, by contrast, has never been weaker. After nine years in power, Emmanuel Macron is a deeply unpopular lame duck, barred from standing in the presidential election due in six months' time. His decision to call a snap election in June 2024 has resulted in a hopelessly gridlocked assembly. Lecornu has described himself as the "weakest prime minister" in living memory and seems unlikely to get a budget through parliament. But that very weakness could prove an asset in his showdown with students. Faced with rising borrowing costs, a deficit of 5.4% of GDP and a public debt at its highest level since the 1940s, Lecornu is financially as well as politically hamstrung. Unlike his predecessors under intense pressure from the street, he has nothing to give. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. title: Zambia signs US health deal after disputes over data-sharing
content: Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US, ending months of public dispute over whether the country was trading citizens' medical data and mineral rights for aid. Under the memorandum of understanding, signed in Lusaka on Thursday along with a data-sharing deal, the US will provide about $1.5bn (£1.1bn), with Zambia also contributing. Civil society groups had criticised a leaked draft they said allowed too much data sharing, while activists seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to minerals, which the then-US ambassador denied. The deal comes after the US Agency for International Development (USAID) was cut. US President Donald Trump had accused USAID of wasteful spending. After closing the agency last year, Washington has pursued similar deals with a number of African countries, arguing partner governments should take on more of the cost. Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda are among those that have signed. Ghana and Zimbabwe have rejected agreements over conditions about sharing data and specimens. Officials say the revised text of Zambia's new deal addresses concerns about privacy, intellectual property and benefit-sharing. Health Minister Roma Chilengi said earlier this week that clauses requiring Zambia to send biological specimens to the US had been removed, and that the agreement would not allow the sharing of individual patient records. Data exchange, he said, would be limited to information needed to monitor and evaluate programmes funded under the deal. A draft leaked earlier this year prompted civil society groups to warn that Zambia was accepting wider data-sharing terms than other African countries, including long-term access to pathogen information and specimens. The Chapter One Foundation, a human rights group, said the government risked "signing away" citizens' health data. HIV advocates, including the Treatment Advocacy and Literacy Campaign, said the flow of information would be one-way and demanded the text be published. Opposition figures and activists also seized on reports that health money was being linked to preferential access for US companies to Zambia's large reserves of copper and other critical minerals. In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe called the data terms a violation of privacy and "unconscionable", and accused Washington of tying the package to minerals. Then-US ambassador, Michael Gonzales, rejected that account as false. The row was sharpened by an earlier US suspension of drug funding after the embassy alleged theft of donated medicines, which the government disputed. Zambia's new deal replaces support that for years flowed largely through US programmes. The money is intended to support HIV/Aids, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance and wider health system work, including the recruitment of community health workers. The US has described the arrangement as a shift from a donor-recipient model towards shared responsibility, with US funding expected to decline over the five years as Zambia increases domestic spending. Officials have put the combined package covering 2026 to 2030 at roughly $3.6bn, though figures for the Zambian share have varied. Shortly after taking office for the second time in January 2025, Trump ordered the closure of USAID, in the process decimating health programmes in some African countries that relied on American funding. Critics say the move has impacted the speed of detecting the current ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and the scale of the response, emphasising that the humanitarian agency was crucial to organising logistics, supplies and local outreach. The US denies its cuts have harmed efforts, arguing that they are more "aligned and effective" under the new arrangement and pointing to the $270m it has donated to tackle the epidemic. Additional reporting by Mallory Moench More than 500 migrants have been expelled from the US to African countries, HRW says, citing US data. The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power. Bernadette Greene-Placentia says her memory of the attack is spotty and that she was knocked unconscious. The distinctive Manhattan skyscraper will undergo a major renovation and provide a new supply of offices. The murderer of Colleen Slemmer is said to be walking and talking in limited ways after two doses of lethal injection. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Italy approves elections overhaul as opposition accuse Meloni of 'scam'
content: Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year. Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government. Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of pushing through the "fraudulent" reform to flout democracy. Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority. Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two. The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation. Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election. A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority. Centre-left members held up signs with slogans including "No to the scam" and "fraudulent law" during a debate ahead of the vote, and accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules. "Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein. Five Star leader and former Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte told AFP news agency that the move was "a mess, a convoluted scheme, devised solely to find a formula to gain an advantage in the upcoming elections". The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia. Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election. "To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens." She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour." Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring. Police say they foiled another school attack on Thursday, and a day after a stabbing at another Polish school. Ukraine accused Russia of targeting two crowded vehicles in the front line city of Kramatorsk to kill as many civilians as possible. In a speech overlooking the Acropolis, the US Secretary of State also said the US believes Europe "can awaken from its long slumber". The step comes after several groups complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers. The order affecting two planned data centres follows concerns over forest clearance. title: Body found in Colombia in search for missing Anton Green
content: The family of a British man missing in Colombia have been told a body has been found in the search for him. Anton Green from Manchester had been living in the South American country for two-and-a-half years, but stopped responding to messages in August. Earlier, his family in Whalley Range were told that a body had been discovered, and that it was believed to be the 43-year-old. They told the BBC that the news - which came just hours after they had renewed their appeal for help finding him - had devastated them and that they were "trying to come to terms with what's happened". A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) spokesman confirmed that the body of a British man had been found in Colombia. Anton's family had told the BBC that his failure to contact his family had been out of character. His mother, Nylva McKie-Williams, had said his last words to her in August were "we will speak at the weekend". She told BBC North West Tonight he had kept in frequent touch with his family, and that it had been "so unlike him not to be in contact with us". Last month, footballer Marcus Rashhford got behind the appeal to find him, describing him as a "family friend". Anton's brother Ro-Shaun Williams had been part of the Manchester United youth team alongside Rashford. Anton's sister Sian Tuohey described her brother as a "happy, decent guy" who had been living in Colombia for three years, having settled there while travelling. He spoke fluent Spanish and, not long before contact was lost, had moved to the Fontibon area of the capital, Bogota. The news of the discovery of a body was broken to the family by police in the early hours of Thursday, the BBC understands. His relatives said they were now waiting on more information from the Attorney General's Office in Bogota. An FCDO spokesman said: "We are aware of the death of a British national in Colombia and are providing support to their family." Listen to the best of BBC Radio Manchester on Sounds and follow BBC Manchester on Facebook , X , and Instagram . You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230. About £100m of climate change projects are being planned in the city to slash emissions. The Church of all Souls in Ancoats was built between 1839-1840 and was a Grade II listed building. Elliot Bulman was jailed after his sexual and physical abuse left a new mother fearing for her life. Michelle Pearson and her four children were murdered in an arson attack at their home in Walkden. title: How toxic haze is causing Singapore’s landmarks to disappear
content: Indonesia is facing one of its worst wildfires seasons, with around one million hectares of land burned so far this year. In Singapore, iconic landmarks are being shrouded in toxic haze from the fires. The BBC’s Tessa Wong is there and breaks down how the wildfire smoke is impacting countries around South East Asia. The municipality building in Baglung was left teetering on an unstable ledge due to floods before it fell into a river. As sellers waded through floodwaters to sell produce like fish and vegetables from floating platforms and foam boxes, buyers walked or paddled between the makeshift stalls to buy their groceries. BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri reports from Delhi, where hundreds of women are protesting. Heavy rain over the last two days has overwhelmed Bangkok's water systems, with more rain forecast on Sunday. Days of near continuous downpours have caused widespread flooding in the Thai capital. The BBC is in Inner Mongolia where dozen of Chinese data centres are being constructed, as the country aims to lead the world in artificial intelligence. Lian Yunzhi broke the women's world record twice in three days at World Cube Association competitions. The typhoon is passing Japan's eastern coast, bringing major disruption and heavy rainfall in its wake. Rescuers are searching for survivors after the vessel travelling from the mainland to a popular tourist destination caught fire. Emergency teams were still searching for at least 86 missing people in the waters off the coast of Coron, in the Philippines. Police say they hope the drill will help prepare students, as concern grows over the increase in school shootings in South East Asia. Chandika Shrestha was airlifted to hospital after spending more than 10 days in her partially buried house. There are still hundreds of workers trapped in a network of tunnels that run along the Trishuli river. Rescuers pull two people from a hydropower tunnel more than a week after a massive flash flood devastated the Nepal-China border. BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri is in Nepal where authorities are trying to begin rebuilding amid the debris. Galaxy Robot Park is a 16,500-square-meter venue in South Korea, with attractions including humanoid robots dancing to K-pop hits. South Asian correspondent Azadeh Moshiri is at the site of a tunnel where rescuers still hope to find survivors following the Nepal-Tibet floods. BBC South Asia correspondent Azadeh Moshiri spoke to a local, who is still waiting for his his wife's body to be retrieved, as rescue efforts continue. Helicopter pilot, Bibek Khadka, has told the BBC that families with missing loved ones have been reaching out to him for help. The BBC's Jonathan Head looks at the historical echoes of US troops arriving in Pattaya, a beach resort famous for its racy bars. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
